title: Customer ticket detail reads return HTTP 500 after application release
customer_impact: Customers can create tickets but ticket-detail reads fail with HTTP 500, preventing them from confirming asynchronous processing and current ticket state.
scope: Failure is isolated to the customer ticket-read path on the newly deployed application release. PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, Nginx, API readiness, and the persisted ticket row remain healthy.

timeline.event: Synthetic/customer validation observed HTTP 500 on GET /api/tickets/<id> after a new release.
L2 acknowledged and confirmed /health/ready plus PostgreSQL, Redis, and RabbitMQ health remained green.
A new ticket was created successfully and the row was confirmed directly in PostgreSQL, ruling out missing business data.
The failing read was correlated by X-Request-ID across Nginx and API logs; the API emitted the simulated RuntimeError and Tempo/Loki contained the same request correlation.
Release comparison isolated the failure to the new API image rather than a shared dependency or proxy outage.
L2 rolled the simulated staging environment back to the known-good release and re-ran the customer journey.
Original ticket detail read returned HTTP 200 and full release verification passed; incident resolved and code defect escalated to development.

evidence: POST /api/tickets succeeds while GET /api/tickets/<id> returns HTTP 500
PostgreSQL, Redis, and RabbitMQ health endpoints remain HTTP 200
persisted ticket row exists in PostgreSQL during the read failure
same failing request ID appears in Nginx and API logs
API logs contain the application RuntimeError for the ticket-read handler
Tempo and Loki contain evidence for the failing request ID
known-good release restores the same ticket read to HTTP 200
complete customer/release verification passes after rollback
resolution: L2 isolated a release-specific API regression rather than changing healthy dependencies. The simulated environment was rolled back to the known-good release, the original ticket read and complete customer journey were re-verified, and the code-level defect was escalated to development for permanent correction.
